result.markdown: # Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions {#i-ep02} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 2, you can - fit and interpret a multiple regression in R - test single coefficients and groups of coefficients against zero - interpret dummy, interaction, and quadratic terms correctly - compare nested models with a partial F-test - read a regression table as printed in a research paper - write a complete analysis that is ready for the exam format and states its limits. ::: Tutorials are **exam preparation sessions**. Every task below follows the format of the final exam. You first try each task in pairs. You may use AI for this, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. Then the solution is discussed together. The tasks follow the order of the course. Task 1 uses Lecture 4, Task 2 uses Lecture 5, and Tasks 3 and 4 use Lecture 6. A regression table then puts the models of Tasks 2 to 4 side by side. Task 5 applies Lectures 3 to 5 to a table in the style of a published paper. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 4 and 5. Lecture 6 is on the day before this tutorial: read its lecture material, and do its practice after the tutorial. Use the complete [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](#intermediate-code-sheet) while working, and review [Mathematics Refresher: multivariable equations, indicators, products, and powers](../resources/math-refresher.html) if needed. Complete from memory: 1. A multiple-regression slope is interpreted while ... 2. A dummy coefficient compares ... 3. An interaction coefficient is a difference in ... 4. A partial F-test compares ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. Holding the other included predictors fixed. 2. A category with the named reference category. 3. Slopes. 4. A reduced nested model with a complete model on the same observations. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial Try each task in R before you open the answer. Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). First build the data for the analysis. The code is the same as in Lectures 4--6: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group), ref = "all_men") known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) ``` ::: ### Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4) Fit: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, data = sharks ) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, data = sharks) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.295 -4.776 -1.283 3.288 82.106 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 22.0249310 0.8878522 24.807 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8361515 0.0509825 -16.401 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028975 0.0005771 -5.021 5.79e-07 *** description_words -0.1283379 0.1137527 -1.128 0.259 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.619 on 1437 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1876, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1859 F-statistic: 110.6 on 3 and 1437 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 1. Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are held fixed. 2. Find out which 95% confidence interval of a coefficient includes zero. 3. Interpret adjusted $R^2$ and the overall F-test. 4. Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer At fixed values of the other included predictors, among the 1,441 recorded pitches: one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less equity offered, an extra \$1,000 requested with about 0.0029 percentage points less (about 0.29 points per \$100,000), and one additional description word with about 0.128 percentage points less. `confint(m1)` shows that the interval for the description words, about $(-0.351, 0.095)$, includes zero. Adjusted $R^2\approx0.186$: the model accounts for about 19% of the variation in the equity offered. The overall F-test ($F\approx110.6$ on 3 and 1437 df) rejects the null hypothesis that all three slopes are zero. Possible reasons against a causal reading: only selected pitches reach the show, the quality of the venture is not measured, the equity offered may influence the amount requested, and the variables may be measured with error. ::: ### Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reduced <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender) summary(complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.118 -4.778 -1.100 3.220 82.590 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 20.8388333 0.5064929 41.143 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8238940 0.0477959 -17.238 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0026613 0.0005822 -4.571 5.28e-06 *** genderall_women 1.2835231 0.4810241 2.668 0.00771 ** gendermixed 0.1209343 0.5411539 0.223 0.82320 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.612 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1913, Adjusted R-squared: 0.189 F-statistic: 84.49 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(reduced, complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1431 83228 2 1429 82792 2 436.25 3.7649 0.0234 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: 1. Name the reference category. 2. Interpret both dummy coefficients. 3. State the hypotheses of the partial F-test and decide. 4. Explain why the partial F-test and the individual t-tests answer different questions. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The reference category is all-men. At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men teams, and mixed teams about 0.12 points more. The unit is percentage points, not percent. The null hypothesis of the partial F-test is that both dummy coefficients are zero. $F\approx3.76$ and p $\approx$ 0.023, so reject at 5%. The two terms are jointly useful, even though the t-test of the mixed dummy alone (p $\approx$ 0.82) is far from significant. The F-test asks whether the two terms together improve the model. Each t-test asks about one comparison with the reference group. The categories are broad and the data do not come from an experiment, so the result does not show a causal effect of gender. ::: ### Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_interaction <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(m_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.871 -4.742 -1.290 3.412 82.689 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 13.6247907 0.3354522 40.616 < 2e-16 *** season_c -0.7993817 0.0663226 -12.053 < 2e-16 *** women 0.8069665 0.4117061 1.960 0.0502 . ask_1k -0.0026776 0.0005834 -4.590 4.83e-06 *** season_c:women -0.0614594 0.0955667 -0.643 0.5203 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.62 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1894, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1871 F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 1. Write the fitted line for `women = 0` and for `women = 1` at a fixed requested amount. 2. Calculate both season slopes. 3. Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value without claiming too much in either direction. 4. Explain what centering does. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer At a fixed requested amount, the fitted line for all-men teams is $13.625-0.799\,season\_c$ plus the term for the requested amount. For teams with women the intercept is $13.625+0.807=14.432$ and the slope is $-0.7994-0.0615=-0.861$. So the season slope is about $-0.799$ percentage points per season for all-men teams and about $-0.861$ for teams with women. The estimated difference in slopes is $-0.061$ percentage points per season with p $\approx$ 0.520. The model gives no evidence that the season trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise. Centering makes the `women` coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8) and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate. ::: ### Task 4: Polynomial term (Lecture 6) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks) m_quadratic <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks ) summary(m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.154 -4.549 -1.011 3.390 82.000 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.171681 0.820566 29.457 < 2e-16 *** season -1.713233 0.205669 -8.330 < 2e-16 *** I(season^2) 0.051034 0.011369 4.489 7.74e-06 *** ask_1k -0.002711 0.000574 -4.723 2.56e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.57 on 1437 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1981, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1965 F-statistic: 118.3 on 3 and 1437 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_linear, m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1438 83493 2 1437 82338 1 1154.5 20.149 7.737e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: 1. Why must `I(season^2)` be used in the R formula? 2. Decide with the partial F-test whether the quadratic term improves the model. 3. Calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11. 4. State why the curve should not be extrapolated beyond Season 16. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer `I()` tells R to calculate the square. Without it, R would read `^` as formula syntax. The partial F-test gives $F\approx20.1$ with p $<$ 0.001, so the quadratic term improves the model. With $\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713$ and $\hat\beta_2\approx0.051$, the change from Season 10 to 11 is $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times10+1)=\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2\approx-0.64$ percentage points. Never read $\hat\beta_1$ alone while the squared term is in the model. Beyond Season 16 the fitted curve turns upward, and no data support that turn. A quadratic curve can change direction sharply outside the observed range. ::: ### The models of Tasks 2 to 4 in one table {#iep02-spec-table} Lecture 4 showed how research papers put several models side by side in one regression table. The table below does this for the models of Tasks 2 to 4. All columns of such a table must use the same observations. Tasks 2 and 3 use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`). Task 4 uses all 1,441 pitches. So first fit the quadratic model again on the 1,434 pitches. The code then prints the two outputs that are not shown above. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_quadratic_known <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(reduced) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.169 -4.814 -1.136 3.277 82.219 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 21.1849717 0.4838230 43.787 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8152726 0.0472948 -17.238 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028517 0.0005776 -4.937 8.87e-07 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.626 on 1431 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.187, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1859 F-statistic: 164.6 on 2 and 1431 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(m_quadratic_known) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.160 -4.540 -1.010 3.401 82.003 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.1677366 0.8217246 29.411 < 2e-16 *** season -1.7128060 0.2059832 -8.315 < 2e-16 *** I(season^2) 0.0509421 0.0113830 4.475 8.24e-06 *** ask_1k -0.0026921 0.0005749 -4.682 3.10e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.576 on 1430 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1982, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1966 F-statistic: 117.9 on 3 and 1430 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Column (1) is the reduced model of Task 2 (`reduced`), column (2) the complete model of Task 2 (`complete`), column (3) the interaction model of Task 3 (`m_interaction`), and column (4) the quadratic model (`m_quadratic_known`). ::: {.reg-table} | | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) | |:---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Season | −0.815\*\*\* | −0.824\*\*\* | −0.799\*\*\* | −1.713\*\*\* | | | (0.047) | (0.048) | (0.066) | (0.206) | | Season squared | | | | 0.051\*\*\* | | | | | | (0.011) | | Amount requested (\$1,000s) | −0.0029\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | | | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | | All-women team | | 1.284\*\* | | | | | | (0.481) | | | | Mixed team | | 0.121 | | | | | | (0.541) | | | | Team with women (all-women or mixed) | | | 0.807 | | | | | | (0.412) | | | Season × team with women | | | −0.061 | | | | | | (0.096) | | | Intercept | 21.185\*\*\* | 20.839\*\*\* | 13.625\*\*\* | 24.168\*\*\* | | | (0.484) | (0.506) | (0.335) | (0.822) | | Observations | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | | $R^2$ | 0.187 | 0.191 | 0.189 | 0.198 | | Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.186 | 0.189 | 0.187 | 0.197 | ::: Outcome: equity offered (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. All four columns use the same 1,434 pitches with a known team classification. The reference group is all-men teams. In column (3) season is centred at its mean (about 8.8), so the intercept and the coefficient of "Team with women" refer to the average season. \* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001. Read along the Season row. The coefficient is close to $-0.8$ in columns (1) to (3). In column (4) it is $-1.713$, because with the squared term in the model the season coefficient alone is not the trend. Read down a column to see one model. Columns (2), (3), and (4) each add terms to column (1), so each can be compared with column (1) by a partial F-test. The bottom rows show that the four models fit almost equally well: adjusted $R^2$ lies between 0.186 and 0.197, a difference of about one percentage point of the variation in the equity offered. Use this layout for regression results in your thesis. ### Task 5: Read a regression table from a paper The table below is invented for this tutorial. It has the layout of a table in a management journal, the same layout as the table above. The outcome is entrepreneurial intention on a scale from 1 to 7, measured in a survey of 265 students. Self-efficacy is a score from 1 to 7 for how confident a student is that he or she can start a business. The intercept is left out, as some journals do. ::: {.reg-table} | | (1) | (2) | |:---|---:|---:| | Age (years) | 0.02 | 0.01 | | | (0.02) | (0.02) | | Female (1 = yes) | −0.21\* | −0.15 | | | (0.10) | (0.10) | | Prior entrepreneurial experience (1 = yes) | | 0.42\*\* | | | | (0.13) | | Entrepreneurial self-efficacy (1--7) | | 0.38\*\*\* | | | | (0.07) | | Observations | 265 | 265 | | $R^2$ | 0.03 | 0.19 | | Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.02 | 0.18 | ::: Outcome: entrepreneurial intention (scale from 1 to 7). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. \* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001. 1. What do the numbers in parentheses and the stars mean? Check the stars of the self-efficacy coefficient with its t statistic. 2. Interpret the self-efficacy coefficient in column (2) in one complete sentence. 3. The coefficient of Female changes from $-0.21$ with a star in column (1) to $-0.15$ without a star in column (2). Explain what happened with the ideas of Lecture 4, and say what the missing star does and does not mean. 4. $R^2$ rises from 0.03 to 0.19. What does that say, and which test would judge whether the two added predictors are jointly useful? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. The numbers in parentheses are standard errors. The stars show the p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against zero. For self-efficacy, $t=0.38/0.07\approx5.4$. This is far beyond the multiplier $t_{0.975,\,260}\approx1.97$, and p is below 0.001, so three stars are correct. 2. Among the 265 surveyed students, a self-efficacy score that is one point higher is associated with an entrepreneurial intention that is 0.38 points higher, holding age, gender, and prior experience fixed. 3. Model (2) holds two more variables fixed than model (1). The Female coefficient now compares women and men with the same experience and self-efficacy. Part of the raw gap of 0.21 points went together with differences in those two variables. The missing star says that the confidence interval around $-0.15$ includes zero. It does not show that the gap is zero. 4. The two added predictors account for a further 16 percentage points of the variation in intentions in this sample. A partial F-test of the two nested models, `anova(reduced, complete)`, would judge whether they are jointly useful. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Timed integrated task: 30 minutes Build one model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) in the Shark Tank file. Use season, the requested amount in \$1,000s, the three known categories of presenting teams, and one extension that you can justify: an interaction or a quadratic term. Your answer must include: 1. a precise research question 2. the code that prepares the data, so that someone else can repeat it 3. one graph of the data before you fit the model 4. the R formula and the model summary. If you compare several models, show them in one regression table in the layout of this tutorial 5. interpretations of the coefficients with units and reference groups 6. a t-test of one coefficient and an overall or partial F-test 7. $R^2$, adjusted $R^2$, and residual diagnostics 8. one graph of fitted values from the model 9. a conclusion of 150 words that keeps apart the association, its uncertainty, and the reasons why it is not causal. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model structure A good solution could fit ```r m <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season * gender + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) ``` or a model with a quadratic term for season and the group dummies. Keep `season` and `gender` in the model next to their interaction (the hierarchy principle), and name the reference group. Interpret slopes that combine several coefficients, or differences between fitted values. Compare the model with a nested reduced model with `anova(reduced, complete)`. Inspect the residuals, including `rstandard()` and Cook's distance, and plot fitted values inside Seasons 1--16. The conclusion must say that the team categories are broad, that only broadcast pitches are in the file, and that the results therefore do not show a causal effect of gender or season. ::: ### Make it yours (5 minutes) :::: {.utility-prompt} Utility: two sentences Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Describe in two sentences the full analysis that you would run on its data. First, name the outcome, two predictors, and one extension (a set of dummies, an interaction, or a quadratic term) that a real question motivates. Second, say which limit you would put first in your conclusion: selection, measurement, or omitted variables. There is no wrong answer. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus (an invented example). "Outcome: weekly orders. Predictors: advertising spend and price, plus a dummy for exam weeks and its interaction with advertising spend, because I believe ads work mainly when students are on campus. The first limit is omitted variables: the weather drives both how many flyers I hand out and how many people are on campus, and nothing in my data measures it." ::: You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with **Tilly**, the course AI assistant. Ask it to review your two sentences before you spend a weekend on the data. :::: QM Intermediate is complete. Review the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](#intermediate-code-sheet), attempt the [QM Intermediate Mock Exam](#intermediate-mock-exam), then return to the [R Refresher](../resources/r-refresher.html), [Mathematics Refresher](../resources/math-refresher.html), or the [External Video Guide](../resources/video-guide.html) whenever you need a targeted review. :::
